title: Thread based dataloading workers
body: ## Context The current PyTorch Dataloader relies on multiprocessing to create n workers. This works well in standard Python as multiprocessing gets us closest to true parallelism in CPU bound tasks because of the GIL. More recently, the dataloading space has been exploring ways to incorporate parallelism using threads ([feature request1](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/158714), [feature request2](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/13246#issuecomment-3097215158), [PyTorch forums](https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/dataloader-using-python-thread-as-opposed-to-multiprocess/86565/2)). This is backed by recent Python-wide development to enable FreeThreaded Python (aka NoGIL) where we can release the GIL to make thread-based development more efficient. We want to explore adding multi-threading support to the PyTorch Dataloader. This would be enabled as straightforwardly as worker_method=threads, with multiprocessing continuing to be the default. Threads based dataloading is not intended to be a drop-in replacement for all use-cases of multiprocessing. It has the potential to outshine when the pipelines leverage native code (for eg torch ops, numpy, FFMPEG decoding, remote I/O, etc) which release the GIL. In those settings, we expect a drop in throughput, but with reduced memory and improved startup time. For jobs that are _model bound_, there should be no drop in throughput. A critical use-case for threading workers is multi-datasets. We expect threads based dataloading to scale to larger dataset counts compared to multi-processing. Our testing supports this hypothesis. ## PR summary / Change list * Refactor existing dataloader * create _ParallelDataLoaderIter, add a threading subclass _ThreadingDataLoaderIter * create _initialize_pin_memory to make it a common utility * Thread local RNG state and WorkerInfo * Each thread worker needs to have its own RNG, as without they risk modifying global random state * These are explicitly made available within WorkerInfo for use in dataset layer * Unit tests * BC is critical here, so keeping almost all of _MultiProcessingDataLoaderIter as is ## Expected changes for end-users * For using thread based dataloading workers, use `worker_method=thread` * Use random generators from `WorkerInfo` in dataset layer or for transforms, i.e. explicitly pass in these generators in random operations. * We are making a change in torchvision to support reading RNG from `WorkerInfo`. ## Benchmarking ### Setup We created a simple benchmark ([dataloader_benchmark.py](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/benchmarks/data/dataloader_benchmark.py) – made some minor modifications to this locally, will push those changes separately) to measure data loading performance. Key metrics being tracked: * Overall throughput * This is samples-per-second from the training loop. This includes data loading time + model fwd and bwd. The results are averaged over 1000 iterations. * CPU memory * For multiprocessing, we track PSS memory of main process + ∑ PSS memory for child process. For threading, we look at RSS memory of the main process. * Specifically, we look at memory-increase: which is the peak memory during the training run minus the memory before the data loader is initialized. * DataLoader initialization time * This is the time spent in dataloader init + getting the iterator (the second step is where the workers are spawned) Machine spec: Single card GPU machine (A100 80GB) with 22 physical CPU cores: 22 and total system memory of 176.56 GB. We fixed the batch_size=64 across all runs. This is a decent batch-size, not too large, not too small. The performance can obviously vary based on batch_size. Dataset: in-memory dataset of dummy tensors, each dataset is 25,000 samples. We use the simple ConcatDataset to put together identical X datasets Transformation pipeline: We use torchvision's v2 transforms and `torchvision.io.read_image`. ``` transform_list = [ transforms.ToDtype( torch.float32, scale=True ), # Convert uint8 to float32 and scale to [0, 1] transforms.Resize(256, antialias=True), transforms.CenterCrop(224), transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]), ] ``` For each datapoint, we run variations with num_workers between (8, 16, 24). We choose the version with higher samples-per-second. This is mimicking optimizing for throughput given X number of datasets. We can see that using thread we can scale to a large number of datasets (because of more memory at disposal), without substantial difference in throughput. Multiprocessing based pipelines do not scale beyond 5 datasets in our benchmarks. They crash with CPU resource constraints. Typically, these are on the lines of: failure to allocate shared memory, CPU OOM, too many file descriptors open, etc With threads, dataloader startup time is a fraction of that of its multiprocessing counterparts. ### Varying batch sizes The plots above track throughput and memory increase against varying batch sizes. Each datapoint on the plot is chosen based on maximum throughput achieved by varying over different num_workers (2,4,6,8,16). The best performing num_worker is annotated on each data point. The number in the yellow box (in 2nd plot) is the ratio of memory increase with multiprocessing over threads. Dataset: ImageNet images read from disk ## FreeThreadedPython To be clear, this feature is stand-alone from the work on FreeThreaded Python, but we would like to show compatibility and benchmark performance with FreeThreaded Python. This is experimental by nature, and would require ensuring all underlying dependencies work smoothly. Changing dataset to files read from local disk. ### Insights * For data loaded in memory, we see significant memory savings (2-3x) with comparable throughput. * For data loaded from disk, there is a slowdown in throughput in regular python builds with GIL (~30%), but with 3.14t (free-threading build) we see comparable throughput to multiprocessing baseline. * Importantly, this shows the improved performance in free threading build. * The main difference between reading from disk vs data pre-loaded in memory are the additional steps of file I/O and image decoding in the former. With increased pre-proc per thread worker, we can expect a relative slowdown. This indicates the need to better understand GIL holding and release in the preprocessing pipeline. * With larger batch sizes and Python 3.14t, we do see crashes sometimes (mostly segmentation faults). That is the reason for the drop off at bs=256 in the plot above. This needs to be investigated. * Tuning num_workers is necessary based on workload. Multiprocessing num_workers=X is not swappable with threading num_workers=X. * In all cases, dataloader startup time with threaded workers costs a tiny fraction compared to multiprocessing. Worth noting: Since the performance will vary depending on the variables of the pipeline (for eg data row size), it is hard to be prescriptive about optimal batch_size or num_workers. ### Design considerations * Thread workers in main process * Similar to multiprocessing workers, we have thread workers in the main process. We went with this design as it supported comparable (or better) performance compared to other variations (listed below). * Worth bringing up, that having all thread workers in the main process _can potentially_ cause interference with main process work aka noisy neighbor problem, in the worst case leading to a slow down kernel scheduling * Thread workers in a separate process * In this design the data loading workers are isolated from the main process. * Cost: IPC cost (but only to a single child process) * Our testing showed that this method was on par or worse with the simpler design of having all workers in the main process. * Single read queue for all workers vs a queue for each worker * Single queue has a simpler design, but can serialize each worker * Cost: * Increased contention for reading * A shared read queue means any worker can pick up the next task, which can be a different worker across different runs. Now, for the cases where we have random transforms in the pipeline, we cannot let _any_ worker pick up a task as that implies that particular worker's random state gets applied in the transform. This will break determinism across identical runs. Same argument for iterable datasets where the dataset sharding is based on worker id. Possibly a blocker. * N read queues provide isolation to each thread (like how it is done in multiprocessing based workers) - ideally should be beneficial in free-threading build * Cost: * more complexity with a layer forwarding indices to n worker queues * Slower workers can slow down job (in case we need batches returned in order - which is the default expectation) * We went ahead with a read queue per worker and a common write queue shared between workers. * Pin memory loop performed inside each worker thread. * We saw improved performance with having each worker pin the batches transforms and collation, instead of leaving this task to another background thread handled by the main process. * Benefit: reduces an extra threading.queue to take in pre-pin_memory batches, and reduces thread contention (specifically useful in non-free-threading builds). * Mini-batching * TL:DR: We can implement a `mini_batch_size` parameter (internal to the implementation, not exposed to the end user) that splits each full batch into smaller mini-batches. These can be processed in parallel by multiple thread workers, then concatenated back into the full batch in the main thread. This can be handled by the _task_info data structure in the main thread (with a new mini_batch_idx key handling dispatching and receiving mini-batches). * Essentially, this means each worker operates at mini_batch_size (which is smaller than batch_size), while the main batch does extra work to prepare the full batch_size before sending it forward to the GPU. * This should further reduce average memory footprint (worst case is same as not splitting the batches at all). But comes at the cost of the main process doing lifting of splitting, concatenating etc. - which requires GIL - taking away potential time from thread workers to do data loading. * More importantly, this approach adds an extra parameter to tune, which isn’t desirable. * With a preliminary implementation we do not see supporting results. * Another considered approach: separate data fetch and data transformations. Spawn a separate process which handles data fetch using X threading workers, shuttles them back to the main process using IPC for transformations by Y threading workers. This can allow each set of thread workers to operate independently; but with the overhead of IPC especially large costs with shuttling un-transformed batches over multiprocessing queues. And like above, this leads to two new parameters which require tuning. ### Note * Also apart from a single GPU setup, we tested this change with a canonical DistributedDataParallel setup on a 1x8 machine (both multiprocessing and threading). * We did test thread-based dataloading with transforms that do not release the GIL - for eg a native python loop computing primes till N. As expected, compared to multiprocessing, using thread based workers has much worse performance. ### Appendix #### Digging into the slowdown at higher batch sizes Looking at `perf stat` counters, there is a clear increase in page faults (specifically minor) when operating at higher batch sizes (like 3072) compared to smaller batch sizes (like 32). With large batches, you're spending disproportionately more time in the kernel space. This can explain the drop in throughput as you increase the batch size. Although, higher page faults are for both threading and multiprocessing workers. Looking at the profiles for threading workers at large batch size (here 3072), there is a significant time spent doing low-level memory management operations like `memset` - specifically this is the kernel trying to allocate memory. Notice the large portion inside `__memset_evex_unaligned_erms` - a highly optimized `memset` implementation from glibc). Now, this is more damaging for threading throughput compared to multiprocessing is that this doesn’t release the GIL, effectively serializing the entire pipeline. Whereas for multiprocessing, each process has an isolated memory space and don’t block on each other. #### Streaming data with HuggingFace (with `load_dataset(...,streaming=True)`) This is a setup where data is streamed over the network with no local cache. Threading workers perform nearly half as fast compared to multiprocessing workers, despite faster startup time and reduced memory footprint. Looking at the profiles, we can see that a significant amount of cycles are spent in managing the reads from remote (i.e. fetching, decoding, deserialization, etc). During this time, the GIL is held which serializes the entire pipeline causing slowdown. There are workarounds to this, like pre-downloading the dataset and streaming from local files; or using a separate process for streaming from remote while populating a bounded queue, which feeds into the dataloader. ## Plan for more benchmarking / testing 1. Varying batch sizes (done) 2. Pipelines with domain specific transforms which cache data 3. Pipelines with transforms leveraging thread specific RNG * TODO: add unit test for this (done) 4. Scaling of multidatasets with lazily-loaded datasets 5. Scaling of datasets with network I/O (for eg streaming HuggingFace dataset) (done) 6. (building on previous one) Dataset with a thread pool doing async IO 7. Platform specific testing (Windows, XPU, etc) * PR CI should cover a lot of it, but there are flows that might run only after merge 8. Testing in FreeThreaded Python build (done) cc @scotts @MalteEbner @vadimkantorov

+    """Dataset that uses thread-specific RNG for deterministic transforms.

+    def __init__(self, loader):

+                "num_workers must be greater than 0 for _ParallelDataLoaderIter"

+                "prefetch_factor must be greater than 0 for _ParallelDataLoaderIter"
+            )
+
+        self._worker_init_fn = loader.worker_init_fn

+        #   Additional worker init function will take care of sharding in MP and Distributed

+                self._worker_init_fn,
+                self._world_size,
+                self._rank,

+        self._workers_done_event: (
+            threading.Event | python_multiprocessing.synchronize.Event | None

+        self._workers: list[Any] = []

+    def _initialize_pin_memory(self):

+        worker method is multiprocessing. For worker_method=thread, pinning

+        """
+        if self._pin_memory:
+            self._pin_memory_thread_done_event = threading.Event()
+

+            self._data_queue = queue.Queue()  # type: ignore[var-annotated]

+                target=_utils.pin_memory._pin_memory_loop,
+                args=(
+                    self._worker_result_queue,
+                    self._data_queue,
+                    current_device_id,
+                    self._pin_memory_thread_done_event,
+                    self._pin_memory_device,

+            # pin_memory_thread once it is started.

+    def _reset(self, loader, first_iter=False):
+        super()._reset(loader, first_iter)

+        self._rcvd_idx = 0  # idx of the next task to be returned in __next__

+        #                  \ (worker_id, data)   if data is already fetched (out-of-order)

+    def _try_get_data(self, timeout=_utils.STATUS_CHECK_INTERVAL):

+        # This can also be used as inner loop of fetching without timeout, with

+    def _failed_worker_error_msg(self, failed_workers) -> str:
+        raise NotImplementedError
+
+    def _check_worker_exception(self) -> None:

+    def _get_data(self):

+        # which we achieve by running `self._try_get_data(timeout=STATUS_CHECK_INTERVAL)`

+    def _next_data(self):

+            # If the worker responsible for `self._rcvd_idx` has already ended
+            # and was unable to fulfill this task (due to exhausting an `IterableDataset`),

+                self._rcvd_idx += 1

+
+            if self._shutdown or self._tasks_outstanding <= 0:

+                )

+            else:
+                worker_id = self._task_info.pop(idx)[0]
+                self._rcvd_idx += 1

+    def _try_put_index(self):

+                    break
+                elif self._workers_num_tasks[worker_queue_idx] < max_tasks // sum(

+                ):

+                    # _workers_status is updated only in this thread, so the sum is guaranteed > 0
+                    break

+            # not found (i.e., didn't break)
+            return
+        self._index_queues[worker_queue_idx].put((self._send_idx, index))  # type: ignore[possibly-undefined]
+        self._task_info[self._send_idx] = (worker_queue_idx,)
+        self._workers_num_tasks[worker_queue_idx] += 1
+        self._tasks_outstanding += 1
+        self._send_idx += 1
+
+    def _process_data(self, data, worker_idx):
+        self._workers_num_tasks[worker_idx] -= 1
+        self._try_put_index()

+            data.reraise()
+        return data
+
+    def _mark_worker_as_unavailable(self, worker_id, shutdown=False):

+        # (2) since we don't join, the worker may still raise error, and we

+    def _shutdown_workers_impl(self) -> None:

+    def __del__(self) -> None:

+class _ThreadingDataLoaderIter(_ParallelDataLoaderIter):
+    r"""Iterates once over the DataLoader's dataset, as specified by the sampler,
+    using threads instead of processes for parallelism.
+
+    Uses per-worker index queues (like multiprocessing mode) to ensure deterministic
+    task-to-worker assignment, which is important for:
+    - Reproducible results with seeded RNG
+    - Consistent behavior with IterableDataset sharding
+    - Matching multiprocessing mode behavior
+    """
+
+    def __init__(self, loader):
+        super().__init__(loader)
+
+        # Thread-based implementation uses standard Python queues
+        self._worker_result_queue = queue.SimpleQueue()  # type: ignore[assignment]
+        self._shutdown = False
+        self._workers_done_event = threading.Event()
+
+        self._index_queues = []
+        self._workers = []
+        for i in range(self._num_workers):
+            # Each worker gets its own index queue (like multiprocessing)
+            # This ensures deterministic round-robin task assignment
+            index_queue: queue.SimpleQueue[Any] = queue.SimpleQueue()
+            w = threading.Thread(
+                target=_utils.worker._thread_worker_loop,
+                args=(
+                    self._dataset_kind,
+                    self._dataset,
+                    index_queue,  # Each thread has its own queue
+                    self._worker_result_queue,
+                    self._workers_done_event,
+                    self._auto_collation,
+                    self._collate_fn,
+                    self._drop_last,
+                    self._base_seed,
+                    self._worker_init_fn,
+                    i,
+                    self._num_workers,
+                    self._pin_memory,
+                ),
+                daemon=True,
+            )
+            w.start()
+
+            self._index_queues.append(index_queue)
+            self._workers.append(w)
+
+        self._data_queue = self._worker_result_queue
+
+        self._reset(loader, first_iter=True)
+
+    def _failed_worker_error_msg(self, failed_workers) -> str:
+        # NOTE: Unlike multiprocessing workers, a fatal signal (e.g., SIGSEGV) in a
+        # thread worker terminates the entire process — this method only handles the
+        # case where a thread exits cleanly but unexpectedly. Fatal crashes bypass this
+        # entirely since the main thread dies along with the worker.
+        thread_ids_str = ", ".join(str(w.ident) for w in failed_workers)
+        return f"DataLoader worker (thread(s) {thread_ids_str}) exited unexpectedly"
+
+    def _shutdown_workers(self) -> None:
+        if _ParallelDataLoaderIter._is_python_exiting():
+            return
+        if not self._shutdown:
+            self._shutdown = True
+            self._shutdown_workers_impl()
+

+class _MultiProcessingDataLoaderIter(_ParallelDataLoaderIter):

+    # NOTE [ Data Loader Multiprocessing Shutdown Logic ]
+    #
+    # Preliminary:
+    #
+    # Our data model looks like this (queues are indicated with curly brackets):
+    #
+    #                main process                              ||
+    #                     |                                    ||
+    #               {index_queue}                              ||
+    #                     |                                    ||
+    #              worker processes                            ||     DATA
+    #                     |                                    ||
+    #            {worker_result_queue}                         ||     FLOW
+    #                     |                                    ||
+    #      pin_memory_thread of main process                   ||   DIRECTION
+    #                     |                                    ||
+    #               {data_queue}                               ||
+    #                     |                                    ||
+    #                data output                               \/
+    #
+    # P.S. `worker_result_queue` and `pin_memory_thread` part may be omitted if
+    #      `pin_memory=False`.
+    #
+    #
+    # Terminating multiprocessing logic requires very careful design. In
+    # particular, we need to make sure that
+    #
+    #   1. The iterator gracefully exits the workers when its last reference is
+    #      gone or it is depleted.
+    #
+    #      In this case, the workers should be gracefully exited because the
+    #      main process may still need to continue to run, and we want cleaning
+    #      up code in the workers to be executed (e.g., releasing GPU memory).
+    #      Naturally, we implement the shutdown logic in `__del__` of

-    # NOTE [ Data Loader Multiprocessing Shutdown Logic ]
-    #
-    # Preliminary:
-    #
-    # Our data model looks like this (queues are indicated with curly brackets):
-    #
-    #                main process                              ||
-    #                     |                                    ||
-    #               {index_queue}                              ||
-    #                     |                                    ||
-    #              worker processes                            ||     DATA
-    #                     |                                    ||
-    #            {worker_result_queue}                         ||     FLOW
-    #                     |                                    ||
-    #      pin_memory_thread of main process                   ||   DIRECTION
-    #                     |                                    ||
-    #               {data_queue}                               ||
-    #                     |                                    ||
-    #                data output                               \/
-    #
-    # P.S. `worker_result_queue` and `pin_memory_thread` part may be omitted if
-    #      `pin_memory=False`.
-    #
-    #
-    # Terminating multiprocessing logic requires very careful design. In
-    # particular, we need to make sure that
-    #
-    #   1. The iterator gracefully exits the workers when its last reference is
-    #      gone or it is depleted.
-    #
-    #      In this case, the workers should be gracefully exited because the
-    #      main process may still need to continue to run, and we want cleaning
-    #      up code in the workers to be executed (e.g., releasing GPU memory).
-    #      Naturally, we implement the shutdown logic in `__del__` of
-    #      DataLoaderIterator.
-    #
-    #      We delay the discussion on the logic in this case until later.
-    #
-    #   2. The iterator exits the workers when the loader process and/or worker
-    #      processes exits normally or with error.
-    #
-    #      We set all workers and `pin_memory_thread` to have `daemon=True`.
-    #
-    #      You may ask, why can't we make the workers non-daemonic, and
-    #      gracefully exit using the same logic as we have in `__del__` when the
-    #      iterator gets deleted (see 1 above)?
-    #
-    #      First of all, `__del__` is **not** guaranteed to be called when
-    #      interpreter exits. Even if it is called, by the time it executes,
-    #      many Python core library resources may already be freed, and even
-    #      simple things like acquiring an internal lock of a queue may hang.
-    #      Therefore, in this case, we actually need to prevent `__del__` from
-    #      being executed, and rely on the automatic termination of daemonic
-    #      children.
-    #
-    #      Thus, we register an `atexit` hook that sets a global flag
-    #      `_utils.python_exit_status`. Since `atexit` hooks are executed in the
-    #      reverse order of registration, we are guaranteed that this flag is
-    #      set before library resources we use are freed (which, at least in
-    #      CPython, is done via an `atexit` handler defined in
-    #      `multiprocessing/util.py`
-    #      https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c606624af8d4cb3b4a052fb263bb983b3f87585b/Lib/multiprocessing/util.py#L320-L362
-    #      registered when an object requiring this mechanism is first
-    #      created, e.g., `mp.Queue`
-    #      https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c606624af8d4cb3b4a052fb263bb983b3f87585b/Lib/multiprocessing/context.py#L100-L103
-    #      https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c606624af8d4cb3b4a052fb263bb983b3f87585b/Lib/multiprocessing/queues.py#L29
-    #      )
-    #
-    #      So in `__del__`, we check if `_utils.python_exit_status` is set or
-    #      `None` (freed), and perform no-op if so.
-    #
-    #      However, simply letting library clean-up codes run can also be bad,
-    #      because such codes (i.e., `multiprocessing.util._exit_function()`)
-    #      include join putting threads for `mp.Queue`, which can be blocking.
-    #      Hence, the main process putting threads are called with
-    #      `cancel_join_thread` at creation.  See later section
-    #      [ 3b. A process won't hang when putting into a queue; ]
-    #      for more details.
-    #
-    #      Here are two example cases where library clean-up codes can run
-    #      before `__del__` is called:
-    #
-    #        1. If we hold onto a reference to the iterator, it more often
-    #           than not tries to do `multiprocessing` library cleaning before
-    #           clearing the alive referenced objects (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/48666)
-    #           and thus prevents our cleaning-up code to run first.
-    #
-    #        2. A similar issue araises when a `DataLoader` is used in a subprocess.
-    #           When a process ends, it shuts the all its daemonic children
-    #           down with a SIGTERM (instead of joining them without a timeout).
-    #           Similarly for threads, but by a different mechanism. This fact,
-    #           together with a few implementation details of multiprocessing, forces
-    #           us to make workers daemonic. All of our problems arise when a
-    #           DataLoader is used in a subprocess, and are caused by multiprocessing
-    #           code which looks more or less like this:
-    #
-    #               try:
-    #                   your_function_using_a_dataloader()
-    #               finally:
-    #                   multiprocessing.util._exit_function()
-    #
-    #           The joining/termination mentioned above happens inside
-    #           `_exit_function()`. Now, if `your_function_using_a_dataloader()`
-    #           throws, the stack trace stored in the exception will prevent the
-    #           frame which uses `DataLoaderIter` to be freed. If the frame has any
-    #           reference to the `DataLoaderIter` (e.g., in a method of the iter),
-    #           its  `__del__`, which starts the shutdown procedure, will not be
-    #           called. That, in turn, means that workers aren't notified. Attempting
-    #           to join in `_exit_function` will then result in a hang.
-    #
-    #           For context, `_exit_function` is also registered as an `atexit` call.
-    #           So it is unclear to me (@ssnl) why this is needed in a finally block.
-    #           The code dates back to 2008 and there is no comment on the original
-    #           PEP 371 or patch https://bugs.python.org/issue3050 (containing both
-    #           the finally block and the `atexit` registration) that explains this.
-    #
-    #
-    #      Finally, another choice is to just shutdown workers with logic in 1
-    #      above whenever we see an error in `next`. This isn't ideal because
-    #        a. It prevents users from using try-catch to resume data loading.
-    #        b. It doesn't prevent hanging if users have references to the
-    #           iterator.
-    #
-    #   3. All processes exit if any of them die unexpectedly by fatal signals.
-    #
-    #      As shown above, the workers are set as daemonic children of the main
-    #      process. However, automatic cleaning-up of such child processes only
-    #      happens if the parent process exits gracefully (e.g., not via fatal
-    #      signals like SIGKILL). So we must ensure that each process will exit
-    #      even the process that should send/receive data to/from it were
-    #      killed, i.e.,
-    #
-    #        a. A process won't hang when getting from a queue.
-    #
-    #           Even with carefully designed data dependencies (i.e., a `put()`
-    #           always corresponding to a `get()`), hanging on `get()` can still
-    #           happen when data in queue is corrupted (e.g., due to
-    #           `cancel_join_thread` or unexpected exit).
-    #
-    #           For child exit, we set a timeout whenever we try to get data
-    #           from `data_queue`, and check the workers' status on each timeout
-    #           and error.
-    #           See `_DataLoaderiter._get_batch()` and
-    #           `_DataLoaderiter._try_get_data()` for details.
-    #
-    #           Additionally, for child exit on non-Windows platforms, we also
-    #           register a SIGCHLD handler (which is supported on Windows) on
-    #           the main process, which checks if any of the workers fail in the
-    #           (Python) handler. This is more efficient and faster in detecting
-    #           worker failures, compared to only using the above mechanism.
-    #           See `DataLoader.cpp` and `_utils/signal_handling.py` for details.
-    #
-    #           For `.get()` calls where the sender(s) is not the workers, we
-    #           guard them with timeouts, and check the status of the sender
-    #           when timeout happens:
-    #             + in the workers, the `_utils.worker.ManagerWatchdog` class
-    #               checks the status of the main process.
-    #             + if `pin_memory=True`, when getting from `pin_memory_thread`,
-    #               check `pin_memory_thread` status periodically until `.get()`
-    #               returns or see that `pin_memory_thread` died.
-    #
-    #        b. A process won't hang when putting into a queue;
-    #
-    #           We use `mp.Queue` which has a separate background thread to put
-    #           objects from an unbounded buffer array. The background thread is
-    #           daemonic and usually automatically joined when the process
-    #           *exits*.
-    #
-    #           In case that the receiver has ended abruptly while
-    #           reading from the pipe, the join will hang forever.  The usual
-    #           solution for this in Python is calling  `q.cancel_join_thread`,
-    #           which prevents automatically joining it when finalizing
-    #           (exiting).
-    #
-    #           Nonetheless, `cancel_join_thread` must only be called when the
-    #           queue is **not** going to be read from or write into by another
-    #           process, because it may hold onto a lock or leave corrupted data
-    #           in the queue, leading other readers/writers to hang.
-    #
-    #           Hence,
-    #             + For worker processes, we only do so (for their output
-    #               queues, i.e., `worker_result_queue`) before exiting.
-    #             + For `pin_memory_thread`, its output queue `data_queue` is a
-    #               `queue.Queue` that does blocking `put` if the queue is full.
-    #               So there is no above problem, but as a result, in
-    #               `_pin_memory_loop`, we do need to  wrap the `put` in a loop
-    #               that breaks not only upon success, but also when the main
-    #               process stops reading, i.e., is shutting down.
-    #             + For loader process, we `cancel_join_thread()` for all
-    #               `_index_queues` because the whole purpose of workers and
-    #               `pin_memory_thread` is to serve the loader process.  If
-    #               loader process is already exiting, we don't really care if
-    #               the queues are corrupted.
-    #
-    #
-    # Now let's get back to 1:
-    #   how we gracefully exit the workers when the last reference to the
-    #   iterator is gone.
-    #
-    # To achieve this, we implement the following logic along with the design
-    # choices mentioned above:
-    #
-    # `workers_done_event`:
-    #   A `multiprocessing.Event` shared among the main process and all worker
-    #   processes. This is used to signal the workers that the iterator is
-    #   shutting down. After it is set, they will not send processed data to
-    #   queues anymore, and only wait for the final `None` before exiting.
-    #   `done_event` isn't strictly needed. I.e., we can just check for `None`
-    #   from the input queue, but it allows us to skip wasting resources
-    #   processing data if we are already shutting down.
-    #
-    # `pin_memory_thread_done_event`:
-    #   A `threading.Event` for a similar purpose to that of
-    #   `workers_done_event`, but is for the `pin_memory_thread`. The reason
-    #   that separate events are needed is that `pin_memory_thread` reads from
-    #   the output queue of the workers. But the workers, upon seeing that
-    #   `workers_done_event` is set, only wants to see the final `None`, and is
-    #   not required to flush all data in the output queue (e.g., it may call
-    #   `cancel_join_thread` on that queue if its `IterableDataset` iterator
-    #   happens to exhaust coincidentally, which is out of the control of the
-    #   main process). Thus, since we will exit `pin_memory_thread` before the
-    #   workers (see below), two separate events are used.
-    #
-    # NOTE: In short, the protocol is that the main process will set these
-    #       `done_event`s and then the corresponding processes/threads a `None`,
-    #       and that they may exit at any time after receiving the `None`.
-    #
-    # NOTE: Using `None` as the final signal is valid, since normal data will
-    #       always be a 2-tuple with the 1st element being the index of the data
-    #       transferred (different from dataset index/key), and the 2nd being
-    #       either the dataset key or the data sample (depending on which part
-    #       of the data model the queue is at).
-    #
-    # [ worker processes ]
-    #   While loader process is alive:
-    #     Get from `index_queue`.
-    #       If get anything else,
-    #          Check `workers_done_event`.
-    #            If set, continue to next iteration

-    #            Otherwise, process data:
-    #                If is fetching from an `IterableDataset` and the iterator
-    #                    is exhausted, send an `_IterableDatasetStopIteration`
-    #                    object to signal iteration end. The main process, upon
-    #                    receiving such an object, will send `None` to this
-    #                    worker and not use the corresponding `index_queue`
-    #                    anymore.
-    #       If timed out,
-    #          No matter `workers_done_event` is set (still need to see `None`)
-    #          or not, must continue to next iteration.
-    #   (outside loop)
+    def __init__(self, loader):
+        super().__init__(loader)
+
+        self._prefetch_factor = loader.prefetch_factor
+        self._in_order = loader.in_order

Suggestion to deal with the typing errors.
1. Create a new type var `TAnyQueue = TypeVar("TAnyQueue", bound=multiprocessing.queues.Queue | queue.Queue)`
2. Make `_ParallelDataLoaderIter` an abstract base class, and give it an abstract method `make_queue(self) -> TAnyQueue`
3. Implement `make_queue` in the subclasses, returning the right type of queue
4. Here in the base class `__init__` you can now do straightforward things like `self._worker_result_queue: TAnyQueue = self.make_queue()`

-    #      being executed, and rely on the automatic termination of daemonic
-    #      children.
-    #
-    #      Thus, we register an `atexit` hook that sets a global flag
-    #      `_utils.python_exit_status`. Since `atexit` hooks are executed in the
-    #      reverse order of registration, we are guaranteed that this flag is
-    #      set before library resources we use are freed (which, at least in
-    #      CPython, is done via an `atexit` handler defined in
-    #      `multiprocessing/util.py`
-    #      https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c606624af8d4cb3b4a052fb263bb983b3f87585b/Lib/multiprocessing/util.py#L320-L362
-    #      registered when an object requiring this mechanism is first
-    #      created, e.g., `mp.Queue`
-    #      https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c606624af8d4cb3b4a052fb263bb983b3f87585b/Lib/multiprocessing/context.py#L100-L103
-    #      https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/c606624af8d4cb3b4a052fb263bb983b3f87585b/Lib/multiprocessing/queues.py#L29
-    #      )
-    #
-    #      So in `__del__`, we check if `_utils.python_exit_status` is set or
-    #      `None` (freed), and perform no-op if so.
-    #
-    #      However, simply letting library clean-up codes run can also be bad,
-    #      because such codes (i.e., `multiprocessing.util._exit_function()`)
-    #      include join putting threads for `mp.Queue`, which can be blocking.
-    #      Hence, the main process putting threads are called with
-    #      `cancel_join_thread` at creation.  See later section
-    #      [ 3b. A process won't hang when putting into a queue; ]
-    #      for more details.
-    #
-    #      Here are two example cases where library clean-up codes can run
-    #      before `__del__` is called:
-    #
-    #        1. If we hold onto a reference to the iterator, it more often
-    #           than not tries to do `multiprocessing` library cleaning before
-    #           clearing the alive referenced objects (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/48666)
-    #           and thus prevents our cleaning-up code to run first.
-    #
-    #        2. A similar issue araises when a `DataLoader` is used in a subprocess.
-    #           When a process ends, it shuts the all its daemonic children
-    #           down with a SIGTERM (instead of joining them without a timeout).
-    #           Similarly for threads, but by a different mechanism. This fact,
-    #           together with a few implementation details of multiprocessing, forces
-    #           us to make workers daemonic. All of our problems arise when a
-    #           DataLoader is used in a subprocess, and are caused by multiprocessing
-    #           code which looks more or less like this:
-    #
-    #               try:
-    #                   your_function_using_a_dataloader()
-    #               finally:
-    #                   multiprocessing.util._exit_function()
-    #
-    #           The joining/termination mentioned above happens inside
-    #           `_exit_function()`. Now, if `your_function_using_a_dataloader()`
-    #           throws, the stack trace stored in the exception will prevent the
-    #           frame which uses `DataLoaderIter` to be freed. If the frame has any
-    #           reference to the `DataLoaderIter` (e.g., in a method of the iter),
-    #           its  `__del__`, which starts the shutdown procedure, will not be
-    #           called. That, in turn, means that workers aren't notified. Attempting
-    #           to join in `_exit_function` will then result in a hang.
-    #
-    #           For context, `_exit_function` is also registered as an `atexit` call.
-    #           So it is unclear to me (@ssnl) why this is needed in a finally block.
-    #           The code dates back to 2008 and there is no comment on the original
-    #           PEP 371 or patch https://bugs.python.org/issue3050 (containing both
-    #           the finally block and the `atexit` registration) that explains this.
-    #
-    #
-    #      Finally, another choice is to just shutdown workers with logic in 1
-    #      above whenever we see an error in `next`. This isn't ideal because
-    #        a. It prevents users from using try-catch to resume data loading.
-    #        b. It doesn't prevent hanging if users have references to the
-    #           iterator.
-    #
-    #   3. All processes exit if any of them die unexpectedly by fatal signals.
-    #
-    #      As shown above, the workers are set as daemonic children of the main
-    #      process. However, automatic cleaning-up of such child processes only
-    #      happens if the parent process exits gracefully (e.g., not via fatal
-    #      signals like SIGKILL). So we must ensure that each process will exit
-    #      even the process that should send/receive data to/from it were
-    #      killed, i.e.,
-    #
-    #        a. A process won't hang when getting from a queue.
-    #
-    #           Even with carefully designed data dependencies (i.e., a `put()`
-    #           always corresponding to a `get()`), hanging on `get()` can still
-    #           happen when data in queue is corrupted (e.g., due to
-    #           `cancel_join_thread` or unexpected exit).
-    #
-    #           For child exit, we set a timeout whenever we try to get data
-    #           from `data_queue`, and check the workers' status on each timeout
-    #           and error.
-    #           See `_DataLoaderiter._get_batch()` and
-    #           `_DataLoaderiter._try_get_data()` for details.
-    #
-    #           Additionally, for child exit on non-Windows platforms, we also
-    #           register a SIGCHLD handler (which is supported on Windows) on
-    #           the main process, which checks if any of the workers fail in the
-    #           (Python) handler. This is more efficient and faster in detecting
-    #           worker failures, compared to only using the above mechanism.
-    #           See `DataLoader.cpp` and `_utils/signal_handling.py` for details.

-    #           For `.get()` calls where the sender(s) is not the workers, we
-    #           guard them with timeouts, and check the status of the sender
-    #           when timeout happens:

-    #               checks the status of the main process.
-    #             + if `pin_memory=True`, when getting from `pin_memory_thread`,
-    #               check `pin_memory_thread` status periodically until `.get()`
-    #               returns or see that `pin_memory_thread` died.
-    #
-    #        b. A process won't hang when putting into a queue;
-    #
-    #           We use `mp.Queue` which has a separate background thread to put
-    #           objects from an unbounded buffer array. The background thread is
-    #           daemonic and usually automatically joined when the process
-    #           *exits*.
-    #
-    #           In case that the receiver has ended abruptly while
-    #           reading from the pipe, the join will hang forever.  The usual
-    #           solution for this in Python is calling  `q.cancel_join_thread`,
-    #           which prevents automatically joining it when finalizing
-    #           (exiting).

-    #           queue is **not** going to be read from or write into by another
-    #           process, because it may hold onto a lock or leave corrupted data
-    #           in the queue, leading other readers/writers to hang.

-    #             + For worker processes, we only do so (for their output
-    #               queues, i.e., `worker_result_queue`) before exiting.
-    #             + For `pin_memory_thread`, its output queue `data_queue` is a
-    #               `queue.Queue` that does blocking `put` if the queue is full.
-    #               So there is no above problem, but as a result, in
-    #               `_pin_memory_loop`, we do need to  wrap the `put` in a loop
-    #               that breaks not only upon success, but also when the main
-    #               process stops reading, i.e., is shutting down.
-    #             + For loader process, we `cancel_join_thread()` for all
-    #               `_index_queues` because the whole purpose of workers and
-    #               `pin_memory_thread` is to serve the loader process.  If
-    #               loader process is already exiting, we don't really care if
-    #               the queues are corrupted.
-    #
-    #
-    # Now let's get back to 1:
-    #   how we gracefully exit the workers when the last reference to the
-    #   iterator is gone.
-    #
-    # To achieve this, we implement the following logic along with the design
-    # choices mentioned above:
-    #
-    # `workers_done_event`:
-    #   A `multiprocessing.Event` shared among the main process and all worker
-    #   processes. This is used to signal the workers that the iterator is
-    #   shutting down. After it is set, they will not send processed data to
-    #   queues anymore, and only wait for the final `None` before exiting.
-    #   `done_event` isn't strictly needed. I.e., we can just check for `None`
-    #   from the input queue, but it allows us to skip wasting resources
-    #   processing data if we are already shutting down.
-    #
-    # `pin_memory_thread_done_event`:
-    #   A `threading.Event` for a similar purpose to that of
-    #   `workers_done_event`, but is for the `pin_memory_thread`. The reason
-    #   that separate events are needed is that `pin_memory_thread` reads from
-    #   the output queue of the workers. But the workers, upon seeing that
-    #   `workers_done_event` is set, only wants to see the final `None`, and is
-    #   not required to flush all data in the output queue (e.g., it may call
-    #   `cancel_join_thread` on that queue if its `IterableDataset` iterator
-    #   happens to exhaust coincidentally, which is out of the control of the
-    #   main process). Thus, since we will exit `pin_memory_thread` before the
-    #   workers (see below), two separate events are used.
-    #
-    # NOTE: In short, the protocol is that the main process will set these
-    #       `done_event`s and then the corresponding processes/threads a `None`,
-    #       and that they may exit at any time after receiving the `None`.
-    #
-    # NOTE: Using `None` as the final signal is valid, since normal data will
-    #       always be a 2-tuple with the 1st element being the index of the data
-    #       transferred (different from dataset index/key), and the 2nd being
-    #       either the dataset key or the data sample (depending on which part
-    #       of the data model the queue is at).
-    #
-    # [ worker processes ]
-    #   While loader process is alive:
-    #     Get from `index_queue`.
-    #       If get anything else,
-    #          Check `workers_done_event`.
-    #            If set, continue to next iteration
-    #                    i.e., keep getting until see the `None`, then exit.
-    #            Otherwise, process data:
-    #                If is fetching from an `IterableDataset` and the iterator
-    #                    is exhausted, send an `_IterableDatasetStopIteration`
-    #                    object to signal iteration end. The main process, upon
-    #                    receiving such an object, will send `None` to this
-    #                    worker and not use the corresponding `index_queue`
-    #                    anymore.
-    #       If timed out,
-    #          No matter `workers_done_event` is set (still need to see `None`)
-    #          or not, must continue to next iteration.
-    #   (outside loop)
+    def __init__(self, loader):
+        super().__init__(loader)
+
+        self._prefetch_factor = loader.prefetch_factor
+        self._in_order = loader.in_order
+
+        if self._num_workers <= 0:
+            raise AssertionError(
+                "num_workers must be greater than 0 for MultiProcessingDataLoaderIter"
+            )
+        if self._prefetch_factor <= 0:
+            raise AssertionError(
+                "prefetch_factor must be greater than 0 for MultiProcessingDataLoaderIter"
+            )
+
+        self._worker_init_fn = loader.worker_init_fn
+
+        # Adds forward compatibilities so classic DataLoader can work with DataPipes:
+        #   Additional worker init function will take care of sharding in MP and Distributed

+                _sharding_worker_init_fn,
+                self._worker_init_fn,
+                self._world_size,
+                self._rank,
+            )
+
+        # Will be set in subclasses
+        self._worker_result_queue = None
+        self._shutdown = False
+        self._workers_done_event = None
+        self._index_queues = []
+        self._workers = []
+        self._data_queue = None

review_comments.body:
There's a technical decision to be made here.  

For process workers, we need to have a thread on the main process which does the memory pinning.  

For thread workers, we could keep the dedicated pin_memory thread, OR we could have the workers do the pin memory themselves.  I'm not sure which one is faster, and it might depend on a bunch of things (num_workers, prefetch_factor, whether or not you've got free threading, etc).  

Seems fine to leave it as is for now (to keep it most similar to the process impl), but might be worth exploring further.

-    #       `done_event`s and then the corresponding processes/threads a `None`,
-    #       and that they may exit at any time after receiving the `None`.
-    #
-    # NOTE: Using `None` as the final signal is valid, since normal data will
-    #       always be a 2-tuple with the 1st element being the index of the data

-    # [ worker processes ]
-    #   While loader process is alive:
-    #     Get from `index_queue`.
-    #       If get anything else,
-    #          Check `workers_done_event`.
-    #            If set, continue to next iteration
-    #                    i.e., keep getting until see the `None`, then exit.
-    #            Otherwise, process data:
-    #                If is fetching from an `IterableDataset` and the iterator
-    #                    is exhausted, send an `_IterableDatasetStopIteration`
-    #                    object to signal iteration end. The main process, upon
-    #                    receiving such an object, will send `None` to this
-    #                    worker and not use the corresponding `index_queue`
-    #                    anymore.
-    #       If timed out,
-    #          No matter `workers_done_event` is set (still need to see `None`)
-    #          or not, must continue to next iteration.
-    #   (outside loop)
+    def __init__(self, loader):
+        super().__init__(loader)
+
+        self._prefetch_factor = loader.prefetch_factor
+        self._in_order = loader.in_order
+
+        if self._num_workers <= 0:
+            raise AssertionError(
+                "num_workers must be greater than 0 for MultiProcessingDataLoaderIter"
+            )
+        if self._prefetch_factor <= 0:
+            raise AssertionError(

+        #   Additional worker init function will take care of sharding in MP and Distributed
+        if isinstance(self._dataset, (IterDataPipe, MapDataPipe)):

+                _sharding_worker_init_fn,
+                self._worker_init_fn,

+                self._rank,

review_comments.body: There's a bunch of logic in here that is specific to multiprocessing.  We should put just the common stuff in here (marking the done event and dealing with the pin_memory thread).  The subclasses should override `_shutdown_workers`, call `super()._shutdown_workers()`, and then do the class-specific stuff.
